en: "May there be no obstacle for you, O Prince, in serving the Lord Guru; you shall attain the state of the Holy One of Great Wisdom. Then he prostrated himself before the Lord, and spoke, saying: "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya. After he had finished his prostration, he spoke again, saying:
For he pervades all beings within this body of embodied souls;

This is the command, O Lord: it must be forgiven, for what else could we do, O Lord? It is because of the true nature of the Holy One who dwells within all beings, who has entered this world, and who is the Lord of the soul of His servants—the very essence of the Lord. For such is the divinity of the Lord; that is why we, Your Highness, prostrate ourselves. The reason we bow before the sandals of our God is that within our own bodies there is a supreme devotion toward the Lord, and our speech is auspicious, so that the children of our God may be blessed.
"What indeed sleeps within this body? What indeed remains awake while [the body] is awake?

What indeed has gone to the ten directions? And what indeed decays as [the body] decays? "It is consciousness (saṃjñā), O Prince, that dwells within the body; it is consciousness that moves about; and it is consciousness that experiences greatness within the body, together with that which suffers within the physical form. "How is it, Prince, regarding the Lord? The God said: "The Lord speaks most excellently; His words are true."
The ten sense organs are asleep; wind and fire remain awake;
the mind has gone to the ten directions; and earth and water decay.

O Prince, that which is called *maturu* consists of the ten sense faculties (*daśendriya*), the mind (*manas*), wind (*vāyu*), and fire (*teja*). This is what is termed the "five winds" (*pañcāvāyu*). Their forms are: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*. This is called the power of fire (*teja-prabhāva*), the brilliance of the body; it is that which moves within the limbs and shines throughout the ten regions [of the body], causing the mind to wander within its own form as an aid to perception. It is that which desires, both worldly and spiritual, its activity being like the movement of a monkey.
One wife, three sons, two ploughs, ten cows,
and a dwelling in Sukṣmetra— whosoever knows this, he shall go to the Sun.

There was one young man, and his sons were three; there was also a bull with ten cows, grazing in the middle of the field. Then, regarding that one young man, the three sons, and that bull with the ten cows, as well as that field which was their property—he brought them all before Lord Śiva, who knows them all, so that he might take possession of them as the sovereign of the entire kingdom.
The wife is clearly the virtues, and the sons are the mind and intellect; the two ploughs are the nine elements and the senses themselves, while the heart is called the field. 5.

Pradhāna is called the single offspring; the three guṇas are called the three offspring, for they arise from Pradhāna. Buddhi and Manas are called the two-fold trunk, or the ten-fold root; the ten indriyas are called the branches; and the heart-vitals (vit) and the vital breaths (puṣupusuh)—all of these together are the objects of cultivation for one who desires liberation.
"Having killed his mother and father, two lions, and two Brahmins;

having destroyed the kingdom and the city, he shall attain the world of Rudra. "Bapanta mvaṅ hibunta / sira patyananta / mvaṅ maliṅ rva / mvaṅ brāhmaṇa rva / ptyananta teka / tlas pjah pva bapanta mvaṅ hibunta / mvaṅ hikaṅ maliṅ rva / lavan ikaṅ brāhmaṇa rva / mvaṅ kaḍatvan lavan varṇṇa mami / kapaṅguh taṅ rudraloka denta / maṅkana liṅ bhaṭara //" "He who kills Bapanta and Hibunta, and likewise Maliṅ Rva and Brāhmaṇa Rva—having slain them all, including those of my own caste—he shall reach the world of Rudra. Such is the meaning of the Lord's words."
One should know Prakṛti as the mother, and they know Puruṣa as the father;

Dharma and Adharma are the two wives, while Buddhi and Manas are the two Brahmins. Prakṛti is designated as the mother; Puruṣa is designated as the father; Dharma and Adharma are designated as the two wives; and Buddhi and Manas are designated as the two Brahmins.
"The ten sense-faculties are indeed the kingdom, and the body is likewise the city.

Having destroyed all these by means of the Self (ātman), one shall attain the world of Rudra. That which is called *siṅguḥ* is the ten sense-faculties; that which is called *vanva* is the body. One must destroy all of these. "Destroy" (*patyanakna*) means: let go of this attachment (*kaliṅan*). Once all power has been relinquished and its attachment has died away, one attains the world of Rudra.

A flower blooms in the sky; fire burns in a river; tortoises have soft backs; and the sun rises at night. (9) "Kill! Strike! Go!"—in the sky; "Sacrificing, [he] does not go to the forest"—in the *daḷm* [script]; "There is that which is hidden, its mountain"; "There is the sun, the lord in the water. This is what he created when he desired to bring forth the world.

What is space, and what is the flower? What is the river, and who indeed is the purifier (fire)? What are the backs of the tortoise, and what is night? Likewise, what is the sun? Another says: "The Lord is space. Another says: "The conch shell is the flower. Another says: "The iron is the river. Another says: "The fire is that which burns within the wind. Another says: "Its peak is the mountain. Another says: "The mountain is called 'vih'. Another says: "The sun is in the mountain."
One's own body is the flower; the mind is remembered as the fire, Oṃkāra.

The ten sense organs are the tortoises, and all the channels (nāḍīs) are remembered as the rivers. (11) This body is that which is called "space" (ākāśa). The divine mind is its stalk. The divine Oṃkāra is the fire within it. The ten sense organs are its roots. That which is called "water" consists of the channels (nāḍīs) of the limbs.
Night should be known as *prakṛti*, and the sun likewise as *puruṣa*.

Having realized the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*), one is liberated; there is no doubt in this. *Saṅ* (She) is *pradhāna*, the head is *vṛtti*; *saṅ* (He) is *puruṣa*, the head is Āditya, the head is the Great One (*mahat*). That which is the *ātman* is hidden within knowledge; having understood all these limbs, one returns to the state of the Lord without doubt.

The aggregates (*skandha*) and the night are to be understood as the eye, and likewise the sun; having realized that the mind is consciousness (*vijñāna*), one is indeed liberated from birth. What is called "the body" (*sinaṅguh vṅi*) here refers to the physical frame composed of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*). What is called "the sun" (*ravi*) refers to the ten sense faculties (*daśendriya*). What is called "the self of knowledge" (*jñānātmā*) is he who has transcended the cycle of birth and rebirth (*janmasaṃsāra*).

The mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), together with the five winds (*vāyu*)—these eight vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are said to be the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) of all beings. Slay that mind; slay that intellect; slay that ego. Furthermore, as for what are called the five winds, their forms are as follows: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*; these are their five divisions.
The eight vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of all beings—
this alone is the aggregate of them all; it is called the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), serving as the life-force of all beings.
Furthermore, that which is called the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) is as follows:
"The chariot" refers to the sense faculties; the "person" (puruṣa) is the charioteer. Righteousness and unrighteousness are the reins; the path is said to be primordial nature (prakṛti).
The chariot means the ten sense faculties. The person is the charioteer. Righteousness and unrighteousness serve as the reins; the Primal Substance (pradhāna) is the axle.
The cart is said to be Viṣṇu, or the bull is the Grandfather (Brahmā);

the Lord (Īśvara) is to be known as the charioteer, while the individual soul (jīva) is within the cart. Indeed, Viṣṇu is the axle; Brahmā is the bull; Īśvara is the head and the charioteer. Lord Śiva is at the top of the chariot; He is the life-force of them all.
The essence of the center of the mandala in the three worlds is three and a half finger-breadths;
situated therein within the three worlds is the manifest image of the mango fruit.
Among those, having thoroughly investigated the supreme triangle, one should divide it into three parts, [determining] the place and the region of the signs. // 17 //

Within this mandala of the three worlds, there exist the realm of Brahmā, the realm of Viṣṇu, and the realm of Rudra. These are directly manifest as the form of the mango fruit (*cūtabimba*). What is its appearance? Within this mango fruit, there is a triangle; that is the abode of Lord Śiva. Furthermore, the lotus situated between the breasts and the navel is called the realm of Brahmā. The realm of Viṣṇu lies spread out above it, and the realm of Rudra is situated at the very top. One must guard it with care; do not let it be defiled, for it is called the supreme region of Brahmā (*brahmadeśa*). Therein resides the primordial source of all things.
And within the bindu, the object of knowledge is indeed eightfold, measuring a thumb’s breadth and possessing exceeding power;
who is the Lord in the heart of the lotus-stalk?
How could one immediately perceive Śiva, who is of the nature of bliss? // 18

This is what is meant by "hana ta vinta" (the state of being one). The thumb-tip of the left hand reaches the region of the heart; this is well-known as that which is called *kāṣṭaiśvarya*. It is in the center of the *ampruh* (the forehead); for that is where Lord Īśvara resides. He is the object of your worship. At that time, you must recite the six-syllable mantra (*ṣaḍvarṇa*): *oṃ sa ba ta a i*. Such is its meaning. Alternatively: *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*. This is what is called the six-syllable mantra. This is the form of those six syllables. He is the one you worship. Once you have finished worshipping Him, you should meditate upon Lord Śiva, who pervades the universe, who is all-pervasive and does not reside in any single place.
The three-fold lotus is considered to be in the heart, at the base, and in the throat;
it gathers all the channels (nāḍīs) like the rays of the sun.
One should strike that lotus in the heart, at the navel, and in the throat—its number is three. It is exceedingly subtle; its opening is upward, and its root is downward.
Having gathered all the channels together, that lotus which is the support for all the channels is placed there; its brilliance is like the radiance of the sun.

The lotus which is in the heart, at its base, is black and very bitter; and that which is extremely black is the "blind black" (*kṛṣṇāndha*), the Lord of the World, the abode of Śiva. The term *kamala* means the *pusuhpusuh* (the heart-lotus). It is situated within the cavity of the heart. The term *kṛṣṇa* (black) is called "bitter" (*tikta*). The term *atikṛṣṇa* (extremely black) refers to all of these together. This is called the "Supreme World" (*paramaloka*), the state of Lord Śiva; He is the object of devotion for the Lord of Yogins.

"Whether it be one's own *liṅga* (*svaliṅga*) or another's *liṅga* (*paraliṅga*), he who makes [it] himself—O twice-born, he dissolves into the *liṅga* of all beings; he dissolves into his own *liṅga*. (21) "Hana ta svaliṅga" means "and the *svaliṅga*, as well as the *paraliṅga*. In brief, there are two kinds of *liṅgas*: that which produces growth and manifests as an external *liṅga* is the *paraliṅga*; that which is the *svaliṅga* is the *liṅga* of all beings (*sarvabhūta*). We have already spoken of this *svaliṅga*, O Kumāra.

That which has arisen spontaneously within the self is called its own characteristic (*svaliṅga*). That which arose previously as the characteristic of another is declared by the wise to be the characteristic of another (*paraliṅga*). (22) "O child, what do you know regarding the self? You are equal to the Omniscient One, for that which is possessed is called the 'characteristic of the self' (*ātma-liṅga*). Because of that characteristic of the self, it is manifest and known by you. What do you know regarding the external characteristic (*bāhya-liṅga*)? That which brings forth this characteristic of the self—know that, O Kumāra."

"A thousand Śiva-liṅgas are not equal to one's own liṅga (ātma-liṅga). There is nothing higher than this; the ātma-liṅga is distinguished as superior. (23) One external liṅga is like a sitting posture (parhyaṅan), a temple, or whatever else one may worship here. All of these together are but a fraction of the ātma-liṅga; they do not even reach it. Indeed, the ātma-liṅga alone is superior to all other liṅgas.
Thousands of *ratnaliṅgas* are not equal to a single *śivaliṅga*;

thousands of *akṣiliṅgas* are not equal to a single *ātmaliṅga*. (24) Why should one worship those *ratnaliṅgas* here? One should worship this single *śivaliṅga*, which is like a thunderbolt; one should worship this *akṣiliṅga*, which is like a thunderbolt; one should worship this single *ātmaliṅga*. This is the teaching (*vaneh*).

The three-syllable word (*tryakṣara*) joined together is declared to be the *oṃkāra*. The mind should abide in the arising of the *liṅga*, the most excellent *śivaliṅga*. The head consists of the three syllables; the feet consist of the four words: the word of Brahmā, the word of Viṣṇu, and the word of Rudra. Its secret name is *oṃkāra*. Therein the mind resides, making Lord Śiva its support in the form of the *liṅga*; that is what is called the *śivaliṅga*. It is not merely this [physical object]. Here is another explanation of it by one who knows: *Tryakṣaraṃ ca padaṃ yuktam oṅkāraḥ samudāhṛtaḥ / liṅgodbhavaṃ manas tiṣṭhec chivaliṅgaṃ mahottamam //* The three-syllable word joined together is declared to be the *oṃkāra*. The head consists of the three syllables; the feet consist of the four words: the word of Brahmā, the word of Viṣṇu, and the word of Rudra. Its secret name is *oṃkāra*. Therein the mind resides, making Lord Śiva its support in the form
For the twice-born, the deity is in the waters; for the sages, in heaven;
for the worlds, the deity is a fragment of stone; and for the munis, the Self alone is the deity.

(26) The Lord is the authority over the *saṅvat* year, O Brāhmaṇa; the Lord is the authority over the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and the month; the Lord is the authority over the *ṛṣi* year; the Lord is the authority over the sky and the month; the Lord is the authority over the world, the tree, and the stone, as well as the image (*pratimā*). Furthermore, the Lord is the authority over the practitioner of yoga (*yogin*), and the Lord is the authority over the venerable Self (*ātman*).
The supreme *puruṣya* is infinite, equal to time (*saṃkāla*), and beyond calculation;

it is the destroyer of the enemies within the *puruṣya*, as well as the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of the moving and the unmoving. (27) "Hana saṅ kālajñāna" means: know the state of the *puruṣa*. That which is called *kālajñāna* is the cause for bringing about [liberation]. Furthermore, there is ignorance (*ajñāna*) which causes the *puruṣa* to fall into *saṃsāra*, causing him to wander through the world of births. "Māyā kajanmasaṅsāra" means: *māyā* is that which causes the self to undergo rebirth. Thus spoke the Lord.

He who worships external signs within his own sign is deluded; and those fools who worship [them] shall obtain only some meager fruit. (28) Those who do not know the inner sign but worship the external sign—they are called fools. Whatever realm they may attain, even though it is indeed a realm, it is still inferior.

Some remember me once; others remember me a hundred times; others remember me constantly. This is their respective task: (29) there are people who remember me once; there are people who remember me a hundred times; there are people who remember me continuously. That which is constant does not lose its purpose; it attains its fulfillment; this is their supreme task. // 29 // *hana ta vvaṅ humaṅĕnaṅĕn aku piṅ śata* (there are people who remember me a hundred times) means that they remember me a hundred times a day. *aku satata* (me continuously) means remembering me at all times, without interruption. *nityaśah ya tan kahilaṅanyārttha* (that which is constant does not lose its purpose) means that because it is performed constantly, it does not fail to achieve its intended goal. *manaṅguh pinakatuturnya* (it attains its fulfillment) means that it reaches its completion. *uttamakāryyanya* (their supreme task) refers to this very practice. // 29 //
The end of the age (*yugānta*) is called the state of dreaming; the end of the age is the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
The fourth state (*turya*) is indeed deep sleep (*suṣupta*), while the northern solstice is said to be the waking state (*jāgrat*).

There is the state of dreaming, which is called the end of the age; this is the southern solstice. There is the state of waking, which is called the northern solstice. There is the state of deep sleep, which is called the fourth state.
The lotus has three stations: the station of dreaming is in the south;
this station of waking is in the north, and the station of deep sleep is in the center.

31. "Kill that lotus; it has three stations: in the west, south, and in the center. The station of dreaming is the southern lotus; the station of waking is the northern lotus; the station of deep sleep is the central lotus."
Endowed with the support of water;
homage be to you, my salutation.
The lotus in the center supports the upper [deity]; the southern lotus and the northern lotus—these are called Bhūmivardhana (?), like a pond with water.

The wise know that the stalk above is three units in measure, or alternatively, three finger-breadths (tryaṅguli) below in measure; this is declared to be the measurement for its position. Three finger-breadths for the joint, three finger-breadths for the ring, and three finger-breadths for the bulb—this is the form of the body of the lotus bud.
The three steps are the three mandalas; the triangle is the triple world.

Therein Śiva delights, and there the Sun (Ravi) fashioned this Māyā. Regarding "the three steps": they are the waking state (*jāgrat-pada*), the deep sleep state (*suṣupta-pada*), and the dream state (*svapna-pada*). Regarding "the three mandalas": there is the triangle (*trikoṇa*) in that place. And in the center of that triangle is the abode of Lord Śiva, where he performs *māyā*; his manifestations are manifold.

The lotus stalk resides in the heart, as do the states of waking and dreaming; indeed, Lord Īśvara, accompanied by all the deities, dwells within that lotus stalk. This is the lotus stalk, which is here in the heart. The state of waking likewise resides here in the heart. Therein is the deity of the lotus stalk, the deity Īśvara, together with all the deities of the body.
The heart of the lotus stalk is said to be the place of deep sleep (*suṣupta*);

know that, O best of sages, it is where the Lord dwells eternally. (35) That which is within the lotus is called the state of deep sleep; that indeed is the abode of the Lord for all time. You, O Kumāra, must realize this.

The form of the fire-element at the navel is like the color of fire; in the heart, it resembles the sun; at the palate, it has the luster of the moon; and within the nose, it possesses the radiance of crystal. (36) The form of the fire-element at the navel is like the color of fire; the form of the fire-element in the heart is like the light of the sun; the form of the fire-element at the palate is like the light of the moon; and the form of the fire-element within the nose is like the brilliance of a crystal gem.
Between the eyebrows, it is like a sapphire; on the forehead, it resembles oil;

on the hand, it should be known as having the luster of silver; and in the center of the head, it is stainless (nirañjana). (37) The interval between the eyebrows is like the radiance of a sapphire; the form of the hand is like the brilliance of silver; and in the center of the head, there exists a stainless light that is beyond description.

Having reached the sphere of space (*ākāśamaṇḍala*), it is called the Gate of Brahmā (*brahmadvāra*). Purified of impurities by fire, they know that which abides in the void to be infinite. As for the sphere of space, its hidden location is the Gate of Brahmā. It is situated within the heart; that which is the Gate of Brahmā is the very center purified by fire. Its essence is pure and corresponds to its own nature. That is the state of the Lord (*bhaṭāra*); that is the supreme station, as stated by the Lord.

"Waking and dreaming are to be known, as well as the state of deep sleep, absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), supreme liberation (*para-kaivalya*), and the seventh space; this is called the 'Seven Spaces' (*saptākāśa*). 39. There is the state of waking (*jāgrat-pada*); there is the state of dreaming (*svapna-pada*); there is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta-pada*); there is the state of the fourth (*turya-pada*); there is the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya-pada*); there is the state of supreme liberation (*parama-kaivalya-pada*); and there is the state of the fourth (*turya-pada*). All these together are designated as the "Seven Spaces" (*saptākāśa*), meaning the seven spaces. Thus spoke the Lord to the Prince.
The Kṛtayuga is said to be the waking state; they know the Tretā to be the state of dreaming;

the Dvāpara is indeed deep sleep, while the Kali is called the fourth state (turya). That which is the waking state is the Kṛta; that which is the state of dreaming is the Tretā; that which is the state of deep sleep is the Dvāpara; and that which is the fourth state is the Kali dissolution (saṃhāra).
"At the root of the navel one is awake; sleep is said to be in the heart;

deep sleep (*suṣupta*) is at the end of the heart; and the fourth state (*turya*) is said here to be in the throat. (41) "In the navel is that which is called the state of waking (*jāgrapada*); in the heart is that which is called the state of dreaming (*svapnapada*); at the tip of the heart is that which is called the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptapada*); and in the throat, at the level of the uvula, is the state called *turyapada*. Such was the teaching of the Lord."
On the forehead is the end of the fourth state (*tūryānta*), and Kaivalya resides in the hands;
on the head is supreme Kaivalya—this is proclaimed as the subtle body (*sūkṣmatanu*).
Thus, this is what is called the seven subtle aggregates (*saptasūkṣmapiṇḍa*).

It is said that the waking state (*jāgrat*) occurs in the forenoon, the dreaming state (*svapna*) at midday, the deep sleep state (*suṣupta*) in the afternoon, and the fourth state (*turya*) here in the night. (43) The state of waking is that which is in the morning; the state of dreaming is that which is at noon; the state of deep sleep is that which is in the evening; and the state of the fourth is that which is at night.

The waking state is white in color; the dream state is like the sun; the deep sleep state resembles the moon; and the fourth state (turya) is like crystal. (44) The color of the waking state is white; the color of the dream state is like that of the sun; the color of the deep sleep state is like that of the moon; and the color of the fourth state is like that of crystal.

The state at the end of the fourth [turyānta] resembles silver; Kaivalya is like gold; the supreme Kaivalya is like the Self; the supreme Kaivalya bestows peace. (45) The color of the end of the fourth is like silver. The color of Kaivalya is like gold. The color of the supreme Kaivalya is luminous. To summarize: the supreme Kaivalya is the state of being liberated from all conceptual constructions (kalpanā).
The waking state is the station of Brahmā, and likewise, the dreaming state is the station of Viṣṇu;
the deep sleep state is the station of Rudra, while Maheśvara is the fourth state (turya).

Hyaṅ Nikaṅ is the waking state; Saṅ Hyaṅ Brahmā [is its presiding deity]. Hyaṅ Nikaṅ is the dreaming state; Saṅ Hyaṅ Viṣṇu [is its presiding deity]. Hyaṅ Nikaṅ is the deep sleep state; Saṅ Hyaṅ Rudra [is its presiding deity]. Hyaṅ Nikaṅ is the fourth state; Saṅ Hyaṅ Maheśvara [is its presiding deity].
The end of the fourth state (*tūryānta*) is Mahādeva, likewise known by the name Śivapada;

and the Kaivalya of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the supreme Kaivalya, which bestows peace. The end of the fourth state is the Lord (*hyaṅ*) Nikaṅ Tūryānta. The Lord Nikaṅ Mahādeva is what is called Śivapada. The Lord Nikaṅ Kaivalya is the Lord Īśāna. The Lord Nikaṅ Paramakaivalya is Bhaṭara Paramaśiva; He is indeed what is called "the Giver of Peace" (*śāntida*), and is designated as Kamokṣan (the One Who Liberates). Such is the description of the Lord, who spoke thus to Kumāra.
The waking state is the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and the dream state is the Vājapeya;

deep sleep is the Puṇḍarīka, and the fourth state is the Rājasūya. (48) The waking stage is that which is the Aśvamedha sacrifice; the dreaming stage is that which is the Vājapeya sacrifice; the deep sleep stage is that which is the Puṇḍarīka; and the fourth stage is that which is called the Rājasūya.
The state of waking is described as follows: he possesses a divine form and has four faces;

he is smeared with ash, wears matted hair, is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), and is wise. (Verse 49) This refers to the waking state. He who performs [this] is indeed the venerable Lord Brahmā. His divine form has four faces; his body is white with ash; he recites the mantras of the four Vedas and wears matted hair. He is a celibate student; he wears the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*). Such is his appearance. He is eternally engaged in worship of the venerable Lord Brahmā.
The deity of the dream emerged, possessing a divine form with four arms;

holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, he had the king of birds as his excellent vehicle. (50) Regarding this verse on the dream: he who performed it was the Lord Viṣṇu. He possessed a divine form, having four heads and four arms. In his hands, he held a conch, a discus, and a mace. He was mounted upon Garuḍa.
The deity described for the state of deep sleep (suṣupta) is Rudra in form, the bearer of Time (Kāladhara).

He is three-eyed, holds a trident in his hand, is Śarva, and has the bull as his vehicle. 51. Regarding this state of deep sleep: the disciple who practices it becomes Lord Rudra; his head is like Time; he possesses three eyes; he bears a trident upon his shoulder; and he stands mounted upon the bull.
And Īśāna is said to be the Lord of the *tūrya* state, eternally satisfied through dispassion;

he is without food, without radiance, and has become like the wind within the moving and the unmoving. (52) O Disciple, the Lord of the Masters, one who practices this *tūrya* state—where is his satisfaction at all times? Its form is as follows: he says, "My father is the wind, which is my own nature within all beings."
At the end of the fourth state (tūrya), he is called Śiva—the seer whose mind is fixed on knowledge.

He who, having known this and himself as well, moves within existence is remembered [as such]. (53) The word "ikaṅ" refers to the state at the end of the fourth. "Ya" means Lord Śiva; "pakupvan" means he is the creator of that being, the ascetic (viku). "Sira" means he possesses this knowledge of the Lord together with the Holy Self (ātmā). "Parananya" means otherwise, at the time of dissolution (pralaya); there is no birth for the Lord, nor is there any possibility of rebirth.

"Mahādeva is indeed the bitter [taste], and Mahājīva is Maheśvara. That which is illusion (*māyā*) in a mirror is declared to be the instruction (*upadeśa*). Indeed, the venerable Mahādeva is the bitter; the venerable Maheśvara is the life-force (*jīva*). What is this illusion? It is seen in the body. Thus says the Lord: 'In this way, O Bhāṭāra, it is the life-force of all beings; it is seen in the body. All of this is what is called the instruction,' so spoke the Lord to the Kumāra."

The Lord (Īśvara) is to be known as Tikta, or Śiva is so proclaimed. Within that [state], there is the vision of ten; therein is the vision of the end of the fourth [state]. O Lord, this is indeed the essence of Tikta. For example, just as the illusion of a worm appears within a cucumber, so too does He appear within the mind. The venerable Īśvara is that Tikta; it is thus.
The *kamala* and the *praṇāla*, as well as the *tīkta*, are indeed the Lord (*īśvara*).

Maheśvara is to be installed there in the divine abode of the body. (56) The *kamala* is one thing; the *praṇāla* is another; the *tīkta* is yet another—that is called the *liṅga*. The body is that which is called the *kahyaṅan*. It is the supreme, divine state of the Lord Maheśvara. He is established in that place. The body is the *pradhāna*; such is the meaning of the word *lavaṅsaṅa*.

Having established Maheśvara, who resembles crystal, within the divine abode of the body—Maheśvara there in the mind—[the question arises: what is that which is measured by the thumb? Its power is that of the Lord (Bhaṭāreśvara). How is it like crystal? The body is said to be similar [to it]. Such is the Lord; thus it is, O Kumāra.

"Let the dull-witted one endure it; thus he spoke this bitter word: 'The king shall become as powerful as the extent of the seven islands. [The Lord said: 'O great sage, regarding that which you have spoken concerning the bitterness of birth—this thumb of yours is like that bitterness. This bitterness does not fit within your thumb, nor within the seven islands. What are these seven islands? Thus spoke the Lord. He is indeed possessed of great power, for there is nothing that can surpass him. Such is the meaning of the *mamuṅguṅ* (the upward-turning); he is called the wise man (*saṅ paṇḍita*) who possesses such speech."
Viṣṇu resides on the left arm and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) on the right;

both Brahmā and Viṣṇu have originated from Maheśvara. The venerable Viṣṇu has his head and face on the right arm; the venerable Brahmā has his head and face on the left arm; Lord Maheśvara has his head and face at the base of the arms of both the venerable Brahmā and Viṣṇu. The venerable Lord is the one who possesses all three. In brief, there are three: the venerable Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; they are the heads of the Lord.
And having become subtle within the heart, it dwells eternally in knowledge. How is its subtlety and its omnipresence to be known? // 60 //

Such is the subtle state of the heart; thus it is known by means of wisdom (*jñāna*). Its location is at the end of the nose, dwelling within the wisdom-organ (*jñānendriya*), united with the Lord (*bhaṭara*). There is emptiness (*śūnya*) arising from emptiness, and there is the stainless (*malit*) arising from the stainless—the supreme liberation (*paramakaivalya*). It is called "without support" (*nirāśraya*); it is not affected by pleasure or pain. Thus spoke the Lord.

The lotus bud within the heart is to be known as the threefold state that grants liberation. Just as all grain depends upon its place for stability, so it is here. There is the lotus, and there is the heart; that which is within the heart is called the "lotus bud. That which is within the heart is called the "heart" itself. When these are combined, they are called the "threefold state," which is the foundation of the entire kingdom.

The heart is pure and auspicious, possessing the rays of thousands of millions of suns; at the end of the heart is the void state, which is called supreme liberation (kaivalya). This is the state where all impurities have been washed away, like water washing away dirt; it serves as the seat for the sun, its radiance completely full and ever-present. This very summit of the heart is the state of voidness; this is what is known as supreme liberation.
"And the function of retention in the heart is the subtle, supreme state of Śiva;

having known that within this body, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. (63) This means: "Strike" (*ikaṅ hati*) refers to the state of Śiva (*śivapada*). This is the *oṃkāra*, which is the supreme void (*paramaśūnya*), and it is also subtle. A person who knows this state of Śiva within the body will have no doubt; thus says the Lord.

A person stands in the terrible ocean of *saṃsāra* like one amidst serpents; having recognized the *Oṃkāra* as Garuḍa, he proceeds toward the half-path of liberation for the sake of self-restraint. (64) The venerable *Oṃkāra* is indeed that Garuḍa who carries away that person from within the water, which is like a pit of fire. He leads that person to the state of Śiva.

One whose self is completely consumed by the fire of the syllable *oṃ* is liberated from the mind; his body, burnt by speech, becomes seedless, bringing an end to birth. (65) The one who has destroyed attachment and pride—that body which is free from affliction—is indeed the venerable *oṃkāra*; he is called "fire."
Among all syllables, the *oṃkāra* is preeminent;

the *oṃkāra* is the supreme, subtle reality that brings about liberation. (66) The venerable *oṃkāra* is indeed the head of all mantras. It is called "supremely subtle" because it is that which attains liberation; the venerable *oṃkāra* serves as the path for the Lord of Yogins.
It is eternally without syllables, devoid of sentient beings, and partless;

it is formless within all existents—this is proclaimed to be liberation (mokṣa). That which is without syllables, that which is non-existent, and that which is within all existents—such as this is subtle; such is the mark of the Lord.
The Self (ātman), the Inner Self (antarātman), and likewise the Supreme Self (paramātman);

the Absolute Self (atyantātman), the All-pervading Lord (vibhu), the Void (śūnya), the Final One (antya), the Ground (bhū), the Ultimate (parama), and Śiva. 68. There exists that which is called the Self; there exists that which is called the Inner Self; there exists that which is called the Supreme Self—these three being within. There exists that which is called the Absolute Self; He is the Lord of the Void, who is designated as Paramaśiva, the Highest Good (niḥśreyasa). Thus one should strive for the realization of the Self.
The Self (ātman) is to be known as Viṣṇu; the inner self (antarātman) is Pitāmaha (Brahmā);
the supreme self (paramātman) is likewise Rudra; and the ultimate, transcendent self is Paramaśiva.
Lord Viṣṇu is the Self; Lord Brahmā is the inner self; Lord Rudra is the supreme self; and Lord Śiva is the ultimate self.
The letter *a* is said to be the waking state, and the letter *u* is indeed the dream state;
the letter *m* is deep sleep, O venerable one, and the syllable *oṃ* is the fourth state (*turya*).

The letter *a* is the seed-syllable of waking; the letter *u* is the seed-syllable of dreaming; the letter *m* is the seed-syllable of deep sleep; and the syllable *oṃ* is the seed-syllable of the fourth state.
Now, there are four locations for the grasping of the syllable *oṃ*;
the wise know them to be at the navel, the heart, the throat, and the head.
(71) "Kill! This is the place of the foot; where is the *oṃ*? The Lord said: "This is the location of the foot. Its form is: the navel, the heart, the throat, and the head."
The isolation of the mind (*manas*) is to be known; the intellect (*buddhi*) is proclaimed as Brahmā;
likewise, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is Rudra, and the quality of goodness (*sattva*) is Maheśvara.
(72) Lord Viṣṇu is the head of the mind; Lord Brahmā is the head of the intellect; Lord Rudra is the head of the ego-sense; and Lord Maheśvara is the head of the quality of goodness.
He is to be known as one who possesses the authority of knowledge, accompanied by the thousand names;
In the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, Oṃkāra is indeed called a boat; for one who has crossed from this shore to the further shore, what further need is there for a boat? (74)

Listen, O Noble One, to that which is to be explained: there is one called Oṃkāra; he is the primordial cause (parahuvanta). He is the ocean, the pure lake. Indeed, the Noble Oṃkāra is the primordial cause. Therefore, when the sins that have accumulated are destroyed, you shall indeed come before the feet of the Lord and be worthy [of Him]; then you will be the primordial cause, for you will no longer have any further purpose, since your purpose has already been fulfilled. It is exactly like that.

One should perceive that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), which abides as the state of subtle knowledge within all beings, in the heart; such is proclaimed as liberation itself. Kill the end of yoga in the heart; kill the subtle, quality-less state. That is where *rajas* and *tamas* are destroyed. Knowledge is the very nature of the instrument of perception; it resides within the body. That which is seen there in the heart is indeed the singular form of the Lord (*Bhaṭara*). That is what is called the "liberation" of the Lord’s sign.

Having burned desire (*kāma*), anger (*krodha*), greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), and even envy (*mātsaryya*) in the fire of the syllable *Oṃ*, one becomes like the moon free from sorrow. [The mantras are: *Kāma* (kahyun), *Krodha* (glĕṅ), *Moha* (puṅguṅ), *Lobha* (kimburu), and *Mātsaryya* (mahyun). O son of Tumuṅgalakna, all these are for worshiping the venerable Lord Brahmā; this is the venerable Lord *Oṃkāra*. He takes away the fire; he purifies all these. Thus, you shall attain the highest bliss (*niḥśreyasa*) and will no longer be stained by impurity (*mala*).

"The instruction composed by the Teacher? Listen, my dear son, for it is one: just as it was taught, so shall you obtain liberation from all sufferings. "What is this noble instruction? Listen, O Prince; I am your father, and you are my son. These words that I speak to you, listen well and act upon them. What is the nature of that knowledge? It is the very form of the fruit you shall attain. Such is the marvelous fragment; how is its nature that it transcends all evil?"

Therefore, for this purpose, one should always and constantly serve the guru; one should act exactly as he instructs, for he is the speaker of the instructions. (78) Indeed, if one has received instruction but does not satisfy [the teacher], it is fruitless. One should possess the marks of a guru; one must be constant in serving the Lord Guru, always offering him respectful service.
Or rather, the body of all the scriptures is the syllable Om itself;
therein lies the secret essence which, when known, one attains peace. (79)

That indeed is the true Guru, who is in accordance with the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*). He is one who bestows the *kalpasan* (the ritual manual); he is worthy of being honored as the teacher. Thus it is that he gives the instruction; let him not desire anything else, for the sacred scripture is his authority. He possesses power (*śakti*) and is the authority of the *madhuparka* offering. He is the venerable *Oṃkāra*, returned from the end of the divine realm. He is the one who knows, the one who is the Lord of the kingdom, and the one who knows the person who is the cause of the teaching; he is the one who possesses the sacred *kalpasan*.

One should know the manifest (vyakta) as primordial nature (prakṛti), and they know the unmanifest (avyakta) as the person (puruṣa). Of these two, they know the manifest to be non-existent (asat) and the unmanifest person to be existent (sat). [Commentary: What is this "one" that is primordial nature? That which is hidden is called the manifest. As for "manifest," it means that there is no duality within it; there exists that which is called the person (puruṣa). His birth is changeless, and his name is primordial nature (prakṛti). He is the principle of your awakening, O Prince.

Just as [the moon] moves by its own natural function like the rays of the moonstone, so too should one remain in the fourth state (*turya*), which is beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. What is the fourth state? It is that which transcends these; waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are those which pass away. This is what is meant by being established in the fourth state: it is like a person who has finished his work and rests, having returned to his own natural function, just as fire returns to its own natural function when the moon rises.

In the world of Rudra, the mother is likewise the Lord (Īśvara), and the father is likewise Mahādeva; those who know the gods understand it thus. He is the venerable Ṛṣi, he is the venerable Īśvara, and he is the venerable Mahādeva, the teacher of all. Such is the nature of the deity as his birth, such is what they know him to be. This is the sign of one who knows the essence of reality.
Night should be known as *prakṛti*, and likewise the sun as *puruṣa*;

Mahādeva is radiance, and Paramaśiva is the void (*śūnya*). That which is within is *prakṛti*; that which is above is *puruṣa*, identified with the sun; the venerable Mahādeva is his splendor; and Lord Śiva is the void. This is the principle of their union.
In great knowledge, the great secret is eternally present within all things;

it is taught that both the manifest and the unmanifest must be relinquished. (84) What is called "great knowledge" (*mahājñāna*) is the cessation of secrecy. It is eternally present within all things whatsoever. That which is manifest and that which is unmanifest—these very things must be abandoned; that indeed is what is meant by "instruction" (*upadeśa*).
In great wisdom, there is the great discourse; from the black flower, Śiva arises. For the sake of awakening grace for the disciples, we give this blessing to you.

(85) All this knowledge is indeed Umaṅĕnaṅĕ; its name is Lord Śiva himself. He is his own abode, and that is the purpose of the Lord: so that one may investigate karma and cultivate virtue, and so that grace may descend upon you here.
In the Great Knowledge (mahājñāna) is the Great Reality (mahātattva); here all doubts are brought to an end.
Śiva resides within the mark of the Self (ātmaliṅga), likewise within the interior of the void of the void (śūnyaśūnyāntara).

(86) *Ṅke saṅ hyaṅ mahājñāna / mahātattva / sira viśeṣa niṅ tattva / samāpta tuḷs tka riṅ dinonya / hayva ta saṅśaya kitānaku saṅ kumāra //* [The mark of] the Great Knowledge / the Great Reality / the specific essence of reality / is completed, equal to that which is other / so that there may be no more doubt for you, O Kumāra.
Śiva resides within the linga of the self;
Lord Śiva dwells within this very linga of the self.
Likewise within the space of emptiness. That which is devoid of any essence is what is called "emptiness."
For here, knowledge is taught in brief, as well as the junction of knowledge;
O sons, grasp with effort this great secret of knowledge. (87)

"Indeed, O Lord Jñāna, that which is secret, I have purified for you, O Kumāra; that which you have sought with great effort, I have bestowed upon you because of your desire for the specific state (*padaviśeṣa*). Such is this condensed Jñāna. Furthermore, there is the *Jñānasandhi*, which you must investigate; it does not lead to rebirth. Thus spoke the Lord, bestowing his supreme favor upon the Kumāra regarding the instruction and the reality of the venerable Ṛṣi. The *Kalpasan* was thus condensed. The Lord and the Goddess departed. //0//
Thus concludes the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, the Great Knowledge, ending with the specific [chapter on] the end. //0//
